definition: A unique ID assigned to an observation by the Ring-Moon Systems Node of the PDS. The OPUS ID is useful for referencing specific observations in a mission-independent manner but should never be used outside of OPUS. To reference an observation outside of OPUS, use the Volume ID, Product ID, and/or Primary File Spec. Note: The format of the OPUS ID is not guaranteed to remain the same over time.
The specific instrument that was used to take the observation. See Help/About for a discussion of the instruments supported by OPUS.

The major planetary mission or project used to take the observation. A mission may be associated with more than one spacecraft, such as Voyager 1 and 2. To search for a specific spacecraft or observatory, use Instrument Host Name. See Help/About for a discussion of the missions supported by OPUS.

The major planetary mission or project used to take the observation. A mission may be associated with more than one spacecraft, such as Voyager 1 and 2. See Help/About for a discussion of the missions supported by OPUS.
The name of the spacecraft, satellite, or ground-based observatory/telescope that took the observation. See Help/About for a discussion of the instrument hosts supported by OPUS.

The planet associated with a given observation. For spacecraft, this corresponds to the phase of the mission, generally indicating which planet the spacecraft was near at the time of the observation. For Hubble, this corresponds to the planet targeted by the observation, if any. To perform more specific searches for observations that have a particular planet in the field of view, use Intended Target Name or Surface Geometry.

The planet associated with a given observation. For spacecraft, this corresponds to the phase of the mission, generally indicating which planet the spacecraft was near at the time of the observation. For Hubble, this corresponds to the planet targeted by the observation, if any.

The specific target(s) representing the observer's intentions. These targets may not actually be in the field of view, and there may be many other targets in the field of view. To search for ANY body in the field of view (but only for some instruments), select Surface Geometry Target Selector under Surface Geometry Constraints in the left menu. To search for observations containing rings, use the Ring Geometry Constraints menu.
The specific target(s) representing the observer's intentions. These targets may not actually be in the field of view, and there may be many other targets in the field of view.
The general class(es) of object(s) indicated by the Intended Target Name(s). Possible values include Planet, Regular Satellite, Irregular Satellite, Ring, Sky, Calibration, and Other.

The time range during which an observation was performed. For compound observations such as spectral cubes or time series, or instruments with multiple detectors like Cassini VIMS, this is the range covered by the entire observation, and may be much longer than the times of the individual component observations. All human activities associated with the observation are considered; for example, for radio occultations the start time is when the first photons leave the spacecraft and the end time is when the last photons arrive at the detector on Earth. Although many formats are supported, the standard is YYYY-MM-DD[Thh:mm:ss.sss]. Both the start and stop time are available as a range, and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.
The time at which the observation started.
The time at which the observation ended.
The time interval during which an observation was performed, equal to the difference between the observation's start time and stop time.

The type of data being measured. Possible values include Reflectivity (the amount of sunlight reflected by a target), Thermal Emission (the electromagnetic radiation from an object due to its temperature), Optical Depth (the amount of light blocked by an object), and Emission (the non-thermal electromagnetic radiation from an object).

Used with Declination to specify a point on the sky. Right ascension is the length of the arc, in degrees, along the celestial equator between the vernal equinox and the point where the hour circle through the point in question intersects the celestial equator, measured eastward in J2000 coordinates. Note that right ascension wraps around from 360 to 0 and thus both minimum and maximum values must be specified for a valid search. OPUS will also allow you to search from a larger number to a smaller number, implying the right ascension must wrap around. Both the minimum and maximum right ascension are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum right ascension of any location in the field of view. Right ascension is the length of the arc, in degrees, along the celestial equator between the vernal equinox and the point where the hour circle through the point in question intersects the celestial equator, measured eastward in J2000 coordinates.

The maximum right ascension of any location in the field of view. Right ascension is the length of the arc, in degrees, along the celestial equator between the vernal equinox and the point where the hour circle through the point in question intersects the celestial equator, measured eastward in J2000 coordinates.

Used with Right Ascension to specify a point on the sky. Declination is the length of the angle measured from the celestial equator to the point in question, measured northward in J2000 coordinates. Both the minimum and maximum declination are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum declination of any location in the field of view. Declination is the length of the angle measured from the celestial equator to the point in question, measured northward in J2000 coordinates.

The maximum declination of any location in the field of view. Declination is the length of the angle measured from the celestial equator to the point in question, measured northward in J2000 coordinates.

The type of data provided by this observation. Possible values include Image (two spatial axes with intensity), Spectrum (zero or one spatial axes with full spectral data at each position), Spectral Image (two spatial axes with partial spectral data at each position, usually formed with a prism or grism), Spectral Cube (two spatial axes with full spectral data at each position), Time Series (one time axis with non-spectral data such as intensity at each time), Spectral Time Series (one time axis with full spectral data at each time), and Occultation Profile (one spatial axis with optical depth at each position).

A unique ID assigned to an observation by the Ring-Moon Systems Node of the PDS. This ID was used by previous versions of OPUS and is only included for backwards compatibility. Please do not use it for new code!
The CIRS focal plane used to obtain the data. Possible values are FP1, FP3 and FP4.

On if any of the interferograms were obtained using 'blinking' mode; Off otherwise. Blinking mode involves alternating between the odd- and even-numbered pixels in FP3 and FP4. Blinking mode is always off for FP1.
On if any of the interferograms were obtained using continuous 'even' mode; Off otherwise. Even mode uses just the even-numbered pixels of FP3 and FP4; it is always off for FP1.
On if any of the interferograms were obtained using continuous 'odd' mode; Off otherwise. Odd mode uses just the odd-numbered pixels of FP3 and FP4; it is always off for FP1.
On if any of the interferograms were obtained using 'centers' mode; Off otherwise. Centers mode uses just the central pixels of FP3 and FP4; it is always off for FP1.

On if any of the interferograms were obtained using 'pairs' mode; Off otherwise. Pairs mode combines the data from adjacent pairs of odd and even pixels in FP3 and FP4: 1+2, 3+4, etc.; it is always off for FP1.

On if any of the interferograms were obtained using 'all' mode; Off otherwise. This mode only refers to the data from FP1, which comprises just a single field of view; it is always off for FP3 and FP4.

The method of conversion used to convert the image from the 12 bits recorded by the camera to the 8 bits recorded in raw file. 12BIT means no conversion, TABLE means conversion by look-up table, and 8LSB means keep only the 8 least significant bits. 12BIT images are highest in geometric precision and are recommended for astrometry.
The type of compression used for the image: Lossless, Lossy, or Not Compressed. Lossy images tend to have subtle artifacts, making them less suitable for astrometry.

The electronics gain setting selected for the image, given in units of electrons per DN. This is an approximate value so both cameras can use the same set of values. Although the Observation Duration is the primary method to maximize signal for faint sources or to prevent saturation of bright sources, the Gain Mode is a complementary tool for the same purposes. Values of the Observation Duration cannot be fully understood without checking the Gain Mode. For example, 1.00-second exposure with a gain of 29 e/DN should have the same signal-to-noise as a 3.28-second exposure with a gain of 95 e/DN.

The purpose(s) of this image: Science, OpNav (optical navigation), Calibration, Support, Engineering, or Unknown. Support images are those associated with a simultaneous observation taken by another instrument. Science, OpNav, and Support images generally include planetary targets; Calibration and Engineering images often do not.

For non-lossy compressed data only, the number of missing or incomplete image lines. For all data, including lossy compressed images, when data is missing, the missing pixel values are replaced by zero. This field is null for lossy compressed data. Search for a maximum of zero missing lines to exclude any images with missing pixels.

An indication of whether this exposure was part of a joint observation with the other ISS camera. NACONLY and WACONLY indicate that only one camera was involved. BOTSIM indicates that both cameras were used simultaneously.
An indication of whether the shutter was enabled during the exposure. Disabled means the shutter remained closed, producing a dark current image rather than a scientific observation.

The seconds portion of the spacecraft clock at shutter close. The image number is included in the image filename. This can be used as an alternate way to limit the time range of selected images or to quickly find a single image.

The summation mode used for this image. FULL indicates a 1024x1024 image. SUM2 indicates as 512x512 image. SUM4 indicates a 256x256 image. Set to FULL to limit your search to images with the most detail.
The name of the intended target for which the exposure was calculated/selected in the given image.

The name of the spectral filter(s) used for the observation. When two filters are combined, the names are joined by a plus sign; the longer wavelength and polarizers always come second. When only one filter name is shown, the other is assumed to be one of the clear filters (CL1 or CL2, as appropriate).
The camera used to take the observation. The Narrow Angle Camera has a field of view of 0.35 degrees and the Wide Angle Camera has a field of view of 3.5 degrees.

The type of observation performed. Values are CALIB (calibration), UCSTAR (atmospheric occultations by cool stars), UFPSCAN (whole sky scans during download), UHDAC (measurement of D/H ratio), UHIGHSN (spectra of rings, atmospheric features, limb, phase coverage), UMAP (Saturn N-S hemispheres, poles, etc.), USCAN (scans of Saturn or the interstellar medium), USTARE (long integrations of Saturn, Titan), and None.
The length of time during which counts were accumulated.

The algorithm used by the instrument to compress data. Values are 8_BIT (only the least significant 8 bits are returned), SQRT_8 and SQRT_9 (small values are returned as-is but larger values are compressed using SQRT), and None (all 16 bits are returned).
The state of the occultation port. Values are Open and Closed.

The width of the slit. Values are High Resolution (75/100 microns for FUV/EUV), Low Resolution (150/200 microns for FUV/EUV), and Occultation (800 microns). The slit for HSP is always 6 microns square. This field is N/A for HSP and HDAC observations.
This indicates whether data was taken from a test pulse.
The length of time the HDAC filament stayed at one voltage level, expressed in multiples of 0.125 ms.
The UVIS channel used. Values are EUV (extreme ultraviolet), FUV (far ultraviolet), HDAC (hydrogen-deuterium absorption cell), and HSP (high speed photometer).
The number of the BAND with the lowest BAND_NUMBER used in this observation.
The number of the BAND with the highest BAND_NUMBER used in this observation.
The number of spectral bands of the instrument that have been summed to produce a single spectral bin in the data file.

The range of line numbers in the window. Both the minimum and maximum line numbers are available as a range, and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.
The minimum line number in the window.
The maximum line number in the window.
The number of spatial bins of the instrument that have been summed to produce a single spatial element in one row of the data file.
The total number of data instances along the horizontal axis (the number of samples in a line).
The mode in which the instrument was acquiring data. Values are IMAGE, LINE, OCCULTATION, POINT, CAL_BACKGROUND, CAL_SOLAR, and CAL_SPECTRAL.
Indicates whether this cube has been reduced to a subset of the bands in the original cube.
Indicates whether this cube has had some bands summed.

When star tracking is off, the VIMS field of view is changed by altering the size or offset of the subset of the array. When star tracking is on, the field of view tracks the brightest pixel in the array as it moves over time. The brightest pixel is set in the instrument by running a previous instrument setup.
The number of pixels (in the X direction) collected during an observation. The angular size of these pixels is dependent upon the sampling mode selected.
The number of slices (in the Z direction) collected during an observation. The angular size of these lines is dependent upon the resolution mode selected.
The exposure time for each pixel in the IR channel.

The spatial resolution mode of the IR channel. Values are Normal (0.5 mrad square pixels), Hi-Res (width 0.25 mrad x length 0.50 mrad), and Under (Nyquist sampling 0.5 mrad square, but with 0.25 mrad overlap along the width axis).
The exposure time for each line in the VIS channel.
The spatial resolution mode of the VIS channel. Values are Normal (0.5 mrad square pixels), Hi-Res (0.167 mrad square), or N/A if the VIS channel is off.
The channel (IR or VIS) used by this observation. Both VIMS channels may be used simultaneously, and the resulting observations are treated as two separated data products in OPUS.

The Galileo activity ID of each image, of the form NNTIOOOOOOMM#SSSXXXX. NN is the orbit number. T is the scan platform target body initial (if applicable). I is the instrument. OOOOOO is the orbit planning guide objective mnemonic. MM is the sequential OAPEL number for each value of NNTIOOOOOO (an OAPEL form is a brief description of the design of the observation). # is the multiple observation flag symbol (- or *). SSS is the PA set number. XXXX is the MIPL (Multimission Image Processing Laboratory) Processing Code.

The image ID, of the form of XXYZZZZ. XX is the orbit (Ax is approach; Cx is cruise). Y is the target body (J=Jupiter, A=Amalthea, I=Io, E=Europa, G=Ganymede, C=Callisto, S=Minor Satellites, R=ring, H=star, L=Moon, W=Earth, V=Venus, U=Ida, P=Gaspra). ZZZZ is the picture count which is generated in the sequence generation process and is incremented separately for each target body in each orbit.

The optical filter used for the image: Clear, Green, Red, Violet, Methane [IR-7270, 0.727 micron], Continuum [IR-7560, 0.756 micron], Methane [IR-8890, 0.889 micron], and Infrared [IR-9680, 0.968 micron].
The optical filter number, containing the unique number associated with the optical filter for the image (0=CLEAR, 1=GREEN, 2=RED, 3=VIOLET, 4=IR-7560, 5=IR-9680, 6=IR-7270, and 7=IR-8890).
The gain mode of the camera. Values are 400K, 100K, 40K, and 10K.
The scan rate of the camera readout in seconds. Values are 2.333, 8.667, 15.166, 30.333, and 60.667.
Identifies if a boom or other type of obstruction was obscuring the view of the camera during the exposure. Values are Possible, Not Possible, or Presence Verified.

The type of compression used for the image. Values are BARC (Block-Adaptive Rate-Controlled, which is lossy and returns a fixed number of 2,592 bits per line), Huffman (lossless), Integer Cosine Transform (lossy), and None. Compressed images (BARC and ICT) tend to have artifacts that make them unsuitable for astrometry.
The type of compression used for the image: Lossless (but compressed), Lossy (using JPEG compression), or Packetized (lossless and uncompressed).
The image binning mode. The options are 1x1 for full resolution (1024x1024 pixels) or 4x4 for reduced resolution (256x265 pixels).
The type of compression used for the image: Lossless (but compressed), Lossy (using JPEG compression), or Packetized (lossless and uncompressed).

The image identifier of the form NNNNES+DDD, where NNNN is the picture sequence number for a given day, E is the planet of encounter (J=Jupiter, S=Saturn, U=Uranus, N=Neptune), S is the Voyager spacecraft (1 or 2), a - sign indicates before and a + sign indicates after closest planetary approach, and DDD is the number of days from closest approach.

The scan rate of the Vidicon readout: '1:1', '2:1', '3:1', '5:1', or '10:1'. The instrument scan rate affects the radiometric properties of the camera because of the dark current buildup on the vidicon.

The instrument shutter mode, one of NAONLY (narrow angle camera shuttered only), WAONLY (wide angle camera shuttered only), BOTSIM (both cameras shuttered simultaneously), BOTALT (both cameras shuttered alternately), BSIMAN (BOTSIM mode followed by NAONLY), or BODARK (shutter remained closed for entire exposure time).
The gain mode (Low or High) of the camera. All Voyager ISS observations in OPUS have a gain mode of Low.
The edit mode of the camera. '1:1' indicates the full resolution of the vidicon while other options indicate partial resolution images.
The optical filter used for the image, one of Clear, Methane-U (CH4_U), Methane-JST (CH4_JS), UV, Violet, Blue, Green, Orange, or Sodium-D (NAD).

The optical filter number (0-7), which contains the unique number associated with the optical filter for the image. It is needed to differentiate between the two CLEAR and two GREEN filters on the Voyager narrow angle camera. For the NAC, 0 and 4 are Clear, 1 is Violet, 2 is Blue, 3 is Orange, 5 and 6 are Green, and 7 is UV. For the WAC, 0 is Methane-JST, 1 is Blue, 2 is Clear, 3 is Violet, 4 is Sodium-D, 5 is Green, 6 is Methane-U, and 7 is Orange. Given the different numberings, this field must be paired with the Camera field to make sense.
The camera used to acquire the image, either Narrow Angle or Wide Angle.
The number of usable lines (Y direction) in the image.
The number of usable samples (X direction) in the image.

The name of the Cassini observation of which the image is a part. Most Cassini observation names include five components, each of which has its own field and definition in OPUS, and thus this field is primarily used to search for complete, specific observation names. The components are the Primary Instrument, the Cassini Orbit Number, the Cassini Target Code, the Cassini Activity Name, and the Instrument Name (that is, the instrument actually used). Within the observation name, the Activity Name is appended by a disambiguating number that is not separately included as a field in OPUS.

The name of the Cassini observation of which the image is a part. Most Cassini observation names include five components, each of which has its own field and definition in OPUS. The components are the Primary Instrument, the Cassini Orbit Number, the Cassini Target Code, the Cassini Activity Name, and the Instrument Name (that is, the instrument actually used). Within the observation name, the Activity Name is appended by a disambiguating number that is not separately included as a field in OPUS.

The number of the orbital revolution of Cassini about Saturn. Orbit numbers change each time the spacecraft goes through its apocenter. For historical reasons, the Cassini orbits are designated 000, 00A, 00B, 00C, 003, 004, 005, and so forth, ending with 293. This search field allows you to select one or more specific orbits, and also allows you to conveniently see how many results there are for each orbit. To search on a range of orbit numbers, see the Saturn Orbit Number (By Range) search field.

The number of the orbital revolution of Cassini about Saturn. Orbit numbers change each time the spacecraft goes through its apocenter. For historical reasons, the Cassini orbits are designated 000, 00A, 00B, 00C, 003, 004, 005, and so forth, ending with 293. This search field allows you to select orbits by numerical range. To search for specific orbits, see the Saturn Orbit Number (By Checkbox) search field.

The number of the orbital revolution of Cassini about Saturn. Orbit numbers change each time the spacecraft goes through its apocenter. For historical reasons, the Cassini orbits are designated 000, 00A, 00B, 00C, 003, 004, 005, and so forth, ending with 293.

An indication of whether the Primary Instrument is the same as the Instrument Name. A value of No indicates that the team of scientists operating the instrument were 'riding' while a different team of scientists controlled the pointing of the spacecraft.

The ID of the instrument whose team of scientists was in charge of pointing the spacecraft during a particular observation. Instrument teams other than the Primary may have found it beneficial to take data even though the design of the observation may not have been attuned to the requirements of their instrument (this is called 'riding').

The spacecraft clock count range during which an observation was performed. The Cassini spacecraft clock count has the format SSSSSSSSS.RRR, where SSSSSSSSS is the number of seconds and RRR is the subRTI component ranging from 0-255. When the shutter was inhibited (i.e. SHUTTER_STATE_ID='DISABLED'), the start and stop clock counts both represent the start of the exposure window during the prepare cycle of the image. This field can be used as an alternative way to limit the time range of observations. Both the start and stop clock counts are available as a range, and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The spacecraft clock count of an observation at shutter open. The Cassini spacecraft clock count has the format SSSSSSSSS.RRR, where SSSSSSSSS is the number of seconds and RRR is the subRTI component ranging from 0-255. When the shutter was inhibited (i.e. SHUTTER_STATE_ID='DISABLED'), the start and stop clock counts both represent the start of the exposure window during the prepare cycle of the image.

The spacecraft clock count of an observation at shutter close. The Cassini spacecraft clock count has the format SSSSSSSSS.RRR, where SSSSSSSSS is the number of seconds and RRR is the subRTI component ranging from 0-255. When the shutter was inhibited (i.e. SHUTTER_STATE_ID='DISABLED'), the start and stop clock counts both represent the start of the exposure window during the prepare cycle of the image.

The time range during which records containing valid data for this image were received on Earth (UTC). Although many formats are supported, the standard is YYYY-MM-DD[Thh:mm:ss.sss]. This field is unlikely to be useful to most researchers.
The time that the earliest record containing valid data for this image was received on Earth (UTC).
The time that the latest record containing valid data for this image was received on Earth (UTC).

The two-letter code identifying the target of the observation as determined by the Cassini team. It is extracted from the second component of the observation name. It indicates the intentions of the science planners, which do not always coincide with what is actually contained in the data product.

The original TARGET_NAME as specified by the appropriate Cassini instrument team. This field does not always indicate which target is actually in the field of view. For that purpose, it is generally better to use Intended Target Name, which has been highly processed by the Ring-Moon Systems Node to more reliably indicate which primary target is in the field of view, or Surface Geometry Target Selector, which can be used to search for any specific body.

A 9-character code name for a set of data products taken during a given time interval. It is an expression of the science planners' intentions. Names were often reused for observations that have similar purposes, though they can also be idiosyncratic. It is extracted from the third component of the observation name, but the disambiguating number at the end is omitted. Examples: GLOBAL, 2x2MOSAIC, FMOVIE.
The mission phase during which an observation was taken.
The segment associated with this data product. This field represents how the mission was planned and is unlikely to be useful to most researchers.

The orbit number around Jupiter. The first character indicates which body had a close flyby during that orbit (Callisto, Europa, Ganymede, Io, Jupiter, or Amalthea). Values range from 0 to 35, although no images were obtained after orbit 33.

The range of spacecraft clock counts for an image. For Galileo SSI, only the spacecraft clock start time is available, so the range consists solely of the time at image acquisition and the Any/All/Only modifiers are not useful. The spacecraft clock is formatted as RRRRRRRR.NN, where RRRRRRRR is an 8-digit number of seconds and NN is a sub-count 0-90.
The spacecraft clock count at the start of image acquisition. The spacecraft clock is formatted as RRRRRRRR.NN, where RRRRRRRR is an 8-digit number of seconds and NN is a sub-count 0-90.

The spacecraft clock count at the end of image acquisition. For Galileo SSI, only the spacecraft clock start time is available, so this field is set to the start of image acquistion. The spacecraft clock is formatted as RRRRRRRR.NN, where RRRRRRRR is an 8-digit number of seconds and NN is a sub-count 0-90.
An identifier for a particular group of data files in the STScI archive.
The numeric identifier of the proposal or observing program, as assigned by STScI.
The name of the Principal Investigator for this HST program, in the form 'last, first, middle initial'.

An abbreviated name or acronym which identifies the instrument's detector used for this observation. WFPC2 generally uses all four of its detectors simultaneously, whereas other HST instruments can use only one detector at a time. As such this field is set to NULL for WFPC2, and instead you should use the fields WFPC2 PC1 Flag, WFPC2 WF2 Flag, WFPC2 WF3 Flag, and WFPC2 WF4 Flag to determine which detector(s) were used in an observation.
The date when the data was last updated by STScI. Although many formats are supported, the standard is YYYY-MM-DD[Thh:mm:ss.sss].
The date when the data was last updated by STScI.
The target of the observation as defined by the Principal Investigator.
The state of the Fine Guidance Sensor on HST, one of Fine, Coarse, Gyros, Fine/Gyro or Unknown.
The name of the filter(s) used for the observation. If two overlapping filters, or a filter and polarizer, were used, then both names are given separated by a plus sign '+'.
The type of the filter (e.g. Narrowband, Medium Band, Long Pass) used for the observation.
The name of the aperture used for the observation.
For STIS, the proposed name of the aperture used for the observation. Only differs from Aperture Type when pseudo-aperture positions are used.
The exposure setting used for the observation, one of Excessive Downtime, Indeterminate, Interrupted, Normal, TDF-Down at Expstart, or Unknown.
The gain state of the instrument used for the observation.
The operating mode of the instrument.
For WFPC2, a flag indicating whether the Planetary Camera (PC1) was used in the observation.
For WFPC2, a flag indicating whether Wide Field #2 (WF2) was used in the observation.
For WFPC2, a flag indicating whether Wide Field #3 (WF3) was used in the observation.
For WFPC2, a flag indicating whether Wide Field #4 (WF4) was used in the observation.
Identifies which of the four CCDs of WFPC2 was pointed at the target.
For STIS, the name of the optical element (grating, mirror, or prism) for the observation.

The spacecraft clock count range during which an observation was performed. The Cassini spacecraft clock count has the format SSSSSSSSS.RRR, where SSSSSSSSS is the number of seconds and RRR is the subRTI component ranging from 0-255. When the shutter was inhibited (i.e. SHUTTER_STATE_ID='DISABLED'), the start and stop clock counts both represent the start of the exposure window during the prepare cycle of the image. This field can be used as an alternative way to limit the time range of observations. Both the start and stop clock counts are available as a range, and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The spacecraft clock count of an observation at shutter open. The New Horizons spacecraft clock count has the format MMMMMMMMMM.SSSSS, where MMMMMMMMMM is the Mission Event Time (MET) and SSSSS is a 5-digit suffix. MET is measured using a 32-bit counter on the New Horizons spacecraft that increments continuously from the beginning of the mission. It runs at a rate of about one increment per second starting from a value of zero at January 19, 2006 18:08:02 UTC, or JD2453755.256337. The partition number is not stored in OPUS, but is 1 through MET 0139810086 and 3 starting at MET 0168423778. No observations in between are archived at the RMS Node. Note that the clock count does not roll over between partitions.

The spacecraft clock count of an observation at shutter close. The New Horizons spacecraft clock count has the format MMMMMMMMMM.SSSSS, where MMMMMMMMMM is the Mission Event Time (MET) and SSSSS is a 5-digit suffix. MET is measured using a 32-bit counter on the New Horizons spacecraft that increments continuously from the beginning of the mission. It runs at a rate of about one increment per second starting from a value of zero at January 19, 2006 18:08:02 UTC, or JD2453755.256337. The partition number is not stored in OPUS, but is 1 through MET 0139810086 and 3 starting at MET 0168423778. No observations in between are archived at the RMS Node. Note that the clock count does not roll over between partitions.
The mission phase during which an observation was taken.
The time at which image data was received on Earth (UTC). This field is unlikely to be useful to most researchers.

The spacecraft clock count range during which an observation was performed. The Voyager spacecraft clock count has the format HHHHH:MM:DDD indicating the 'FDS' or 'Flight Data System' count. HHHHH is a five-digit 'FDS hour' (equal to 48 true minutes, numbered 0-65535), MM is 2-digit 'FDS minute' (equal to 48 true seconds, numbered 0-59), and DDD is a 3-digit 'FDS tick' which increments every 60 msec, numbered 1-800.

The spacecraft clock count of an observation at shutter open. The Voyager spacecraft clock count has the format HHHHH:MM:DDD indicating the 'FDS' or 'Flight Data System' count. HHHHH is a five-digit 'FDS hour' (equal to 48 true minutes, numbered 0-65535), MM is 2-digit 'FDS minute' (equal to 48 true seconds, numbered 0-59), and DDD is a 3-digit 'FDS tick' which increments every 60 msec, numbered 1-800.

The spacecraft clock count of an observation at shutter close. The Voyager spacecraft clock count has the format HHHHH:MM:DDD indicating the 'FDS' or 'Flight Data System' count. HHHHH is a five-digit 'FDS hour' (equal to 48 true minutes, numbered 0-65535), MM is 2-digit 'FDS minute' (equal to 48 true seconds, numbered 0-59), and DDD is a 3-digit 'FDS tick' which increments every 60 msec, numbered 1-800.
The mission phase during which an observation was taken.

The PDS4 bundle or PDS3 volume containing the observation. PDS4 bundles are semantically-meaningful constructs used to group similar observations; the bundle name is descriptive and part of the LID for each included data product. PDS3 volumes are artificial constructs used to group consecutive observations into manageable chunks. They are formatted as MMIII_NNNN, where MMIII is an abbreviation for the mission and instrument (e.g. COISS for Cassini Orbiter ISS) and NNNN is a four-digit volume number. Hubble volumes have 5-digit volume numbers and are formatted as HSTIN_NNNN. See Bundles/Volumes under Help for the list of bundles and volumes available in OPUS.

A string assigned by the PDS describing a PDS3 data set. Data sets are often aggregations of multiple volumes. A Data Set ID usually encodes, at a minimum, the mission, instrument, and version number of the data as provided by the instrument team.
A permanent identifier assigned to a PDS3 data product by the PDS that is unique within its data set.

A Logical IDentifier assigned to a PDS4 data product. While each individual data product has its own LID, the LID used here is the one identified by OPUS as the primary data product. If searching by LID, it may be most productive to perform a partial string search on the LID prefix.
The approximate date and time when the PDS data product was created for inclusion in the archive. Although many formats are supported, the standard is YYYY-MM-DD[Thh:mm:ss.sss].
The approximate date and time when the PDS data product was created for inclusion in the archive.
The full primary data product filename, including the path, relative to its containing bundle/volume in the PDS archive.
Miscellaneous notes or comments about an observation, such as why the observation was taken or known problems with the data.

An occultation is a measurement in which a source signal passes through a medium before being observed. Radio means the source is an artificially-emitted radio signal. Solar means the source is the Sun. Stellar means the source is a star other than the Sun. A reflectance profile is a measurement in which a source signal is reflected from a surface and a 1-D slice is recorded.

Ingress means that, from the observer's point of view, the source moves inward from the periphery toward the center of the medium. Egress means the source moves outward. Both means the source moves both inward and outward within a single observation.
A flag indicating whether the source passes behind a any planet or other body as seen by the observer during the observation.
The time interval between each sample in the original source observation(s).
A subjective rating of quality of the occultation or reflectance profile.

The range of optical depths detectable within the observation. Negative values indicate the signal was too poor to allow calculation. The minimum optical depth detectable within the observation. Negative values indicate the signal was too poor to allow calculation.
The maximum optical depth detectable within the observation. Negative values indicate the signal was too poor to allow calculation.
The wavelength band at which an observation was made.
The name of the star or artificial transmitter that emitted the source signal.
The name of the observatory or spacecraft at which the signal was observed.

The range of ring longitudes (based on the ascending node) in the field of view. Ring longitude specifies the inertial longitude of the ring plane intercept point. The range of solar hour angles in the field of view. Solar hour angle specifies the longitude of the ring plane intercept point relative to the anti-solar direction. At 90 degrees, the ring particles are moving toward the Sun, whereas at 270 degrees they are moving away. Ring intercept points that are obscured by the planet or a moon within the observed field of view are ignored. However, ring intercept points that are shadowed by the planet are not ignored. Note that solar hour angle wraps around from 360 to 0 and thus both minimum and maximum values must be specified for a valid search. OPUS will also allow you to search from a larger number to a smaller number, implying the solar hour angle must wrap around. Both the minimum and maximum solar hour angles are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

This column tabulates the minimum value of solar hour angle within the field of view of the observation. For fields of view that cross the midnight meridian, the tabulated minimum value will be greater than the maximum.

The range of ring azimuths in the field of view. Ring azimuth is the angle measured at a point in the ring plane, starting from the direction of a photon heading to the observer, and ending at the direction of a local radial vector. This angle is projected into the ring plane and measured in the prograde direction. As seen from the observer, it equals 90 degrees along the right ansa and 270 degrees along the left ansa. Note that this quantity differs from ring longitudes for viewpoints relatively close to the rings, because angles are measured at the ring intercept point rather than at the center of the planet. Ring intercept points that are obscured by the planet or a moon within the observed field of view are ignored. For observations capturing reflected sunlight (i.e., with wavelengths in the visual or near-infrared), ring intercept points that are shadowed by the planet are also ignored. Note that ring azimuth wraps around from 360 to 0 and thus both minimum and maximum values must be specified for a valid search. OPUS will also allow you to search from a larger number to a smaller number, implying the ring azimuth must wrap around. Both the minimum and maximum ring azimuths are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

In practice, it defines the approximate size of the smallest linear feature that can be resolved if that feature is oriented optimally on the surface. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. For observations capturing reflected sunlight (i.e., with wavelengths in the visual or near-infrared), the night side of the target body is also ignored.

The maximum finest surface resolution in the field of view, in other words the smallest resolvable feature that could be resolved anywhere in the field of view provided that feature is oriented optimally on the surface. Finest surface resolution is the shorter dimension of a pixel as projected onto the surface at the intercept point. In practice, it defines the approximate size of the smallest linear feature that can be resolved if that feature is oriented optimally on the surface. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. For observations capturing reflected sunlight (i.e., with wavelengths in the visual or near-infrared), the night side of the target body is also ignored.

The range of coarsest surface resolutions in the field of view. Coarsest surface resolution is the longer dimension of a pixel as projected onto the surface at the intercept point. At any given intercept point, the coarsest surface resolution is typically larger than the finest resolution by a factor of 1/cos(emission angle). In practice, this defines the approximate size of a linear feature that can be resolved if that feature has its worst possible orientation on the surface. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. For observations capturing reflected sunlight (i.e., with wavelengths in the visual or near-infrared), the night side of the target body is also ignored. Both the minimum and maximum coarsest surface resolutions are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum coarsest surface resolution in the field of view, in other words the size of the smallest feature that could be resolved somewhere within the field of view, even if its orientation on the surface is the worst it can be. Coarsest surface resolution is the longer dimension of a pixel as projected onto the surface at the intercept point. At any given intercept point, the coarsest surface resolution is typically larger than the finest resolution by a factor of 1/cos(emission angle). In practice, this defines the approximate size of a linear feature that can be resolved if that feature has its worst possible orientation on the surface. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. For observations capturing reflected sunlight (i.e., with wavelengths in the visual or near-infrared), the night side of the target body is also ignored.

The maximum coarsest surface resolution in the field of view, in other words the size of the smallest feature that could be resolved anywhere in the field of view and regardless of its orientation on the surface. Coarsest surface resolution is the longer dimension of a pixel as projected onto the surface at the intercept point. At any given intercept point, the coarsest surface resolution is typically larger than the finest resolution by a factor of 1/cos(emission angle). In practice, this defines the approximate size of a linear feature that can be resolved if that feature has its worst possible orientation on the surface. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. For observations capturing reflected sunlight (i.e., with wavelengths in the visual or near-infrared), the night side of the target body is also ignored.

The range of linear sizes of a pixel as projected at the distance of the planet or specified target body in the observation. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The minimum linear size of a pixel as projected at the distance of the planet or specified target body in the observation. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The maximum linear size of a pixel as projected at the distance of the planet or specified target body in the observation. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The range of phase angles at the center of the planet or specified target body in the observation. This is the angle between the local direction of in incoming photon from the Sun and the local direction of an outgoing photon to the observer. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The minimum phase angle at the center of the planet or specified target body in the observation. This is the angle between the local direction of in incoming photon from the Sun and the local direction of an outgoing photon to the observer. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The maximum phase angle at the center of the planet or specified target body in the observation. This is the angle between the local direction of in incoming photon from the Sun and the local direction of an outgoing photon to the observer. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The range of phase angles in the field of view. Phase angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the direction of the incoming photon from the Sun and the direction of the outgoing photon to the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored. Both the minimum and maximum phase angles are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum phase angle in the field of view. Phase angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the direction of the incoming photon from the Sun and the direction of the outgoing photon to the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored.

The maximum phase angle in the field of view. Phase angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the direction of the incoming photon from the Sun and the direction of the outgoing photon to the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored.

The range of incidence angles in the field of view. Incidence angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the local surface normal vector and the direction of the incoming photon from the Sun. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored. Both the minimum and maximum incidence angles are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum incidence angles in the field of view. Incidence angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the local surface normal vector and the direction of the incoming photon from the Sun. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored.

The maximum incidence angles in the field of view. Incidence angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the local surface normal vector and the direction of the incoming photon from the Sun. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored.

The range of emission angles in the field of view. Emission angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the local surface normal vector and the direction of the outgoing photon to the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored. Both the minimum and maximum emission angles are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum emission angle in the field of view. Emission angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the local surface normal vector and the direction of the outgoing photon to the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored.

The maximum emission angle in the field of view. Emission angle is the angle, measured at the surface intercept point, between the local surface normal vector and the direction of the outgoing photon to the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored.

The range of local hour angles in the field of view. Local hour angle is a measure of the local solar time as observed at the surface intercept point on the planet or a specified target body. The value is 180 degrees at a point on the surface as the Sun is crossing the local meridian. Local hour angle can alternatively be understood as a longitude frame that originates at the anti-solar direction and increases toward the east (assuming prograde rotation). The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored. Note that right local hour angle wraps around from 360 to 0 and thus both minimum and maximum values must be specified for a valid search. OPUS will also allow you to search from a larger number to a smaller number, implying the local hour angle must wrap around. Both the minimum and maximum local hour angles are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum local hour angle in the field of view. Local hour angle is a measure of the local solar time as observed at the surface intercept point on the planet or a specified target body. The value is 180 degrees at a point on the surface as the Sun is crossing the local meridian. Local hour angle can alternatively be understood as a longitude frame that originates at the anti-solar direction and increases toward the east (assuming prograde rotation). The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored. For fields of view that cross the midnight meridian, the tabulated minimum value will be greater than the maximum.

The maximum local hour angle in the field of view. Local hour angle is a measure of the local solar time as observed at the surface intercept point on the planet or a specified target body. The value is 180 degrees at a point on the surface as the Sun is crossing the local meridian. Local hour angle can alternatively be understood as a longitude frame that originates at the anti-solar direction and increases toward the east (assuming prograde rotation). The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. The night side of the target body is not ignored. For fields of view that cross the midnight meridian, the tabulated minimum value will be greater than the maximum.

The projected direction of the body's pole vector on the sky, measured as an angle clockwise from celestial north (i.e., toward celestial west). This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The projected direction of the body's pole vector on the sky, measured as an angle counterclockwise from celestial north (i.e., toward celestial east). This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The range of limb clock angles in the observation. Limb clock angle is the companion coordinate to limb altitude. It measures the angle as projected on the sky from the body's north pole to the surface normal from the limb. The angle is measured in a clockwise direction. Limb points where the altitude is outside the range -0.1 to 3 times the body's radius are not included in the tabulation. The body's shape has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or a targeted body are ignored. Note that limb clock angle wraps around from 360 to 0 and thus both minimum and maximum values must be specified for a valid search. OPUS will also allow you to search from a larger number to a smaller number, implying the limb clock angle must wrap around. Both the minimum and maximum limb clock angles are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum limb clock angle in the observation. Limb clock angle is the companion coordinate to limb altitude. It measures the angle as projected on the sky from the body's north pole to the surface normal from the limb. The angle is measured in a clockwise direction. Limb points where the altitude is outside the range -0.1 to 3 times the body's radius are not included in the tabulation. Note that for data products that capture both sides of clock angle zero, this value will be numerically greater than the 'maximum' clock angle. The body's shape has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or a targeted body are ignored.

The maximum limb clock angle in the observation. Limb clock angle is the companion coordinate to limb altitude. It measures the angle as projected on the sky from the body's north pole to the surface normal from the limb. The angle is measured in a clockwise direction. Limb points where the altitude is outside the range -0.1 to 3 times the body's radius are not included in the tabulation. Note that for data products that capture both sides of clock angle zero, this value will be numerically greater than the 'maximum' clock angle. The body's shape has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or a targeted body are ignored.

The range of limb altitudes in the observation. Limb altitude is the perpendicular distance between a pixel's line of sight and the nearest point on the body's limb. Negative values refer to lines of sight interior to the limb. Limb altitudes outside the range -0.1 to 3 times the body's radius are not included in the tabulation.

The minimum limb altitude in the observation. Limb altitude is the perpendicular distance between a pixel's line of sight and the nearest point on the body's limb. Negative values refer to lines of sight interior to the limb. Limb altitudes outside the range -0.1 to 3 times the body's radius are not included in the tabulation.

The maximum limb altitude in the observation. Limb altitude is the perpendicular distance between a pixel's line of sight and the nearest point on the body's limb. Negative values refer to lines of sight interior to the limb. Limb altitudes outside the range -0.1 to 3 times the body's radius are not included in the tabulation.

The apparent diameter of the body in pixels. It is computed for the body at its true distance, but as if it fell at the center of the field of view, with its longest axis perpendicular to the line of sight. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The position of the center of the body in the image in the X or sample direction. A fractional value of 0.5 indicates the center of the pixel. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The position of the center of the body in the image in the Y or line direction. A fractional value of 0.5 indicates the center of the pixel. This value is defined by the geometry during the time of the observation; it is independent of the field of view.

The range of surface intercept times. The surface intercept time is the time the photon leaves the body surface before being received by the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. Both the minimum and maximum surface intercept times are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The earlier surface intercept time in the observation. The surface intercept time is the time the photon leaves the body surface before being received by the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. Both the minimum and maximum surface intercept times are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The latest surface intercept time in the observation. The surface intercept time is the time the photon leaves the body surface before being received by the observer. The surface has been modeled as an ellipsoid. Surface intercept points that are obscured by the planet or another moon within the observed field of view are ignored. Both the minimum and maximum surface intercept times are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The type of camera used. In a Frame camera, all pixels are exposed simultaneously. In a Pushbroom camera, the image is obtained by sweeping a single line of pixels across the target. In a Raster Scan camera, the image is constructed by repeatedly sweeping a single pixel across a field of view.

The time interval between the opening and closing of an instrument aperture (such as a camera shutter). For most instruments this is the same as Observation Duration. For Cassini UVIS this is the integration duration. For Cassini VIMS this is the exposure duration for the given detector.

The number of discrete values that can appear in a single data point. This is a property of the instrument and does not represent the actual contents of the observation. For example, a camera with 12-bit pixels will support 4096 levels.
For an observation that can be represented as a 2-D array of pixels, this is the number of pixels along the longer of the two axes.
For an observation that can be represented as a 2-D array of pixels, this is the number of pixels along the shorter of the two axes.

The range of wavelengths at which an observation was made. For spectrographic instruments, this is the actual range available. For most imaging instruments, this is the full transmission bandwidth. For Cassini ISS, this is based on the FWHM around the center wavelength. Some instruments natively use wavelength and others natively use wavenumber. OPUS supports both quantities for all instruments and searches over equivalent ranges of wavelength and wavenumber will produce identical results. Both the minimum and maximum wavelengths are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum (shortest) wavelength at which an observation was made. For spectrographic instruments, this is the actual minimum. For most imaging instruments, this is the full transmission bandwidth. For Cassini ISS, this is based on the FWHM range around the center wavelength.

The maximum (longest) wavelength at which an observation was made. For spectrographic instruments, this is the actual maximum. For most imaging instruments, this is the full transmission bandwidth. For Cassini ISS, this is based on the FWHM range around the center wavelength.

The range of widths of spectral lines that can be reliably detected in an observation, measured in wavelengths. For most non-spectrographic instruments, this is equal to the filter bandpass. For Cassini ISS, it is equal to the FWHM. Both the minimum and maximum wavelength resolutions are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The smallest distance between spectral lines that can be reliably detected in an observation, measured in wavelengths. For most non-spectrographic instruments, this is equal to the filter bandpass. For Cassini ISS, it is equal to the FWHM.

The largest distance between spectral lines that can be reliably detected in an observation, measured in wavelengths. For most non-spectrographic instruments, this is equal to the filter bandpass. For Cassini ISS, it is equal to the FWHM.

The range of wavenumbers at which an observation was made. The wavenumber is the reciprocal of the wavelength, i.e., the number of waves per unit of length. This quantity is provided to support instruments that measure spectra in uniformly-spaced steps of wavenumber rather than wavelength. Some instruments natively use wavelength and others natively use wavenumber. OPUS supports both quantities for all instruments and searches over equivalent ranges of wavelength and wavenumber will produce identical results. Both the minimum and maximum wavenumbers are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.

The minimum wavenumber (corresponding to the longest wavelength) at which an observation was made. The wavenumber is the reciprocal of the wavelength, i.e., the number of waves per unit of length. This quantity is provided to support instruments that measure spectra in uniformly-spaced steps of wavenumber rather than wavelength, although both wavenumber and wavelength are provided for all instruments.

The maximum wavenumber (corresponding to the shortest wavelength) at which an observation was made. The wavenumber is the reciprocal of the wavelength, i.e., the number of waves per unit of length. This quantity is provided to support instruments that measure spectra in uniformly-spaced steps of wavenumber rather than wavelength, although both wavenumber and wavelength are provided for all instruments.

The range of widths of spectral lines that can be reliably detected in an observation, measured in wavenumbers. Both the minimum and maximum wavenumber resolutions are stored for each observation and the search can be made more specific using the any/all/only modifiers. See Help/FAQ for more information.
The smallest distance between spectral lines that can be reliably detected in an observation, measured in wavenumbers.
The largest distance between spectral lines that can be reliably detected in an observation, measured in wavenumbers.

A flag indicating whether an observation contains separable information about multiple wavelengths. The flag is Yes for spectrographic instruments and imaging cameras using prisms or grisms as long as there is more than one spectral bin.
The number of distinct wavelengths or wavelength bins that can be detected in an observation. Null for non-spectrographic instruments not using prisms or grisms.
The type of polarization detected by the instrument. Values are Linear (linear polarization) or None (no polarization filter used).

Raw image files (*.IMG) for Cassini ISS. Images are in VICAR format, uncalibrated, and in units of DN (data number). Associated labels (*.LBL) are text files that contain information about the image.
